summary: Specifies version 4 of the Network File System protocol, which lets computers use files stored on remote servers as if they were local. Unlike earlier versions, it integrates file locking and replaces the separate MOUNT protocol. It builds on NFS versions 2 and 3.

plainLanguage.summary: NFS (Network File System) version 4 lets a client access files and folders stored on a server through one protocol. It combines file access, locking, security negotiation, and file-system navigation, while batching operations to reduce separate requests. This RFC defines NFSv4 minor version 0 and replaces RFC 3530.

questions: what is a compound request in nfsv4
subtitle: How NFSv4 combines remote file access, locking, security, and caching in one protocol.

tldr.problem: Earlier NFS versions relied on a separate MOUNT protocol and did not include byte-range locking in NFS itself. NFSv4 also aims to work well across Internet links and support stronger security and internationalized names.
tldr.mechanism: NFSv4 uses two RPC procedures, including COMPOUND requests that carry ordered file operations. It integrates locking and namespace traversal, negotiates security per filehandle, and allows clients to cache data under defined rules.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7530 replaces RFC 3530 as the definition of NFSv4 minor version 0 without invalidating previously valid requests. The unit metadata says RFC 7530 was updated by RFC 7931 and RFC 8587.

today: RFC 7530 is a Proposed Standard and, according to the unit metadata, was updated by RFC 7931 and RFC 8587. It obsoletes RFC 3530 as the definition of NFSv4, and defines minor version 0.

sections.title: Goals and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 7530 defines NFS version 4 (NFSv4), a distributed file system protocol built on NFS versions 2 and 3 (RFC 1094 and RFC 1813). A client uses it to access files held by a server. The protocol keeps the earlier versions' focus on recovery, independence from transport and operating systems, simplicity, and performance.

The RFC sets goals for better operation across the Internet, including firewall traversal, high-latency and low-bandwidth links, and many clients per server. It also calls for stronger security with negotiation, cross-platform interoperability, and extensions that preserve backward compatibility. Together with RFC 7531, it replaces RFC 3530; it does not make previously valid requests invalid.
sections.plainLanguage: NFSv4 lets a computer work with files held on a remote server. It was designed to combine file access with locking and security, and to work across different systems and Internet conditions.

sections.title: Combining Operations into One Request
sections.content:
NFSv4 has two Remote Procedure Call (RPC) procedures: NULL and COMPOUND. A COMPOUND request carries an ordered list of operations, such as LOOKUP, OPEN, and READ. A client can combine those three operations to read a file in one request, even without earlier contact with the server.

The server runs the operations in order and stops when one fails. It returns results for the operations it already evaluated. Operations share a current filehandle, which identifies the file-system object being used, and can also save a second filehandle for some operations. A COMPOUND request is not a transaction: earlier operations may have succeeded when a later one fails, so clients must handle partial completion.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can place several file operations in one request, and the server processes them in order. If one operation fails, later ones do not run, and earlier work is not automatically undone.

sections.title: Filehandles, Attributes, and Access
sections.content:
A filehandle is a server-specific identifier for a file-system object. The client treats its contents as opaque and sends it back when referring to that object. NFSv4 defines persistent filehandles, which remain valid for the object's lifetime, and volatile filehandles, which may expire. The fh_expire_type attribute tells the client which behavior to expect.

File metadata is represented by attributes. Every client and server must support REQUIRED attributes, while RECOMMENDED attributes may be unavailable; clients can ask which attributes a server supports. Named attributes are byte streams associated with a file or directory and accessed through OPENATTR. The RECOMMENDED access control list (ACL) attribute lets a server evaluate ordered ALLOW and DENY entries to decide whether a request has permission.
sections.plainLanguage: A filehandle is an identifier that lets a client refer to an object without interpreting the identifier itself. Attributes describe objects, and each server reports which optional attributes it supports.

sections.title: One Namespace Across File Systems and Servers
sections.content:
NFSv4 removes the need for a separate MOUNT protocol to obtain the first filehandle. A client starts from a server's root filehandle and follows names with LOOKUP. The server can present its exports as one browsable namespace, using a read-only pseudo-file system to bridge gaps between exported file systems.

The fs_locations attribute can identify other server addresses and paths for a file system. A present file system can list alternatives for replication or migration. An absent file system contains only its root; ordinary access returns NFS4ERR_MOVED, while a client can request location information to find the file system. A location for a file system that was not present is called a referral.
sections.plainLanguage: The server can show its exported folders as one connected tree, even when they belong to separate file systems. It can also direct a client to another server when a file system is absent or has another listed location.

sections.title: Transport and Security Negotiation
sections.content:
NFSv4 uses RPC version 2 and External Data Representation (XDR) to encode protocol data. Port 2049 SHOULD be the default. When NFSv4 runs over IP, its transport MUST be an IETF-standardized protocol specified to avoid network congestion; TCP and SCTP are examples, and every implementation MUST support TCP.

Implementations MUST support RPCSEC_GSS and the Kerberos V5 security mechanism, including authentication, integrity, and privacy services, although using RPCSEC_GSS is optional. Authentication identifies a user principal rather than only trusting the client machine. Security can vary by filehandle: after NFS4ERR_WRONGSEC, a client can use SECINFO to learn acceptable choices. The RFC recommends protecting security negotiation and file-location replies with integrity, because an attacker could alter them.
sections.plainLanguage: NFSv4 requires implementations to support Kerberos V5 through RPCSEC_GSS, but administrators are not required to use that mechanism. The client can ask which security method a file needs, and integrity protection helps prevent an attacker from changing that answer.

sections.title: Open State, Locks, and Leases
sections.content:
NFSv4 includes byte-range locks and share reservations, so the server keeps state about clients. A client establishes its identity with SETCLIENTID and SETCLIENTID_CONFIRM. The server returns a client ID. It identifies each open, lock, or delegation with a stateid, which is a 128-bit value made of a 96-bit other field and a 32-bit sequence ID.

The server groups a client's state under a lease with a fixed duration. Client operations can renew the lease, or the client can use RENEW. If a client cannot renew before the lease expires, the server may release its locks. After a server restart, a grace period lets clients reclaim state; during that period the server normally rejects ordinary reads, writes, and new lock requests until recovery is safe.
sections.plainLanguage: The server tracks file opens and locks under a lease, which lasts for a fixed time set by the server. After a restart, clients can reclaim their previous locks during a recovery period before ordinary access resumes.

sections.title: Client Caching and Delegations
sections.content:
NFSv4 lets clients cache attributes and directory information for periods they choose, then check the server for changes. A client checks file data when it opens a file and must send modified data to the server before closing a write-open file. Locking and share reservations constrain caching so that cached data does not break the access rules applications rely on.

At an open, the server may grant a recallable delegation. A read delegation assures the client that other clients cannot write the file; a write delegation assures that other clients cannot read or write it. The client can then handle some operations locally. If a conflicting request arrives, the server calls back to recall the delegation, and the client must send modified state and return it. A server grants delegations only when the callback path works, and clients cannot assume they will receive one.
sections.plainLanguage: A client may keep file information locally, but it must check for changes and send modified data back at the required points. A delegation lets the client handle some work locally until the server recalls that permission for another client's request.

sections.title: Internationalized Names
sections.content:
NFSv4 generally represents strings that may contain non-ASCII characters using UTF-8, including file and directory names. The RFC recognizes that a client or server may interact with file systems that use other encodings, and it allows servers to accept component names that are not valid UTF-8.

The protocol does not require one Unicode normalization form. Clients and servers may therefore encounter names that use different forms, and a server may choose how to normalize or compare names. The RFC warns that changing names without knowing their encoding can make files inaccessible or cause different names to be treated as equivalent.
sections.plainLanguage: NFSv4 prefers UTF-8 for file and folder names, but some servers may accept other encodings. It does not require one way to normalize Unicode names, so clients and servers must handle differences carefully.

sections.title: Minor Versions and Named Attributes
sections.content:
This RFC defines NFSv4 minor version 0. The protocol's minor-version rules say that each future minor version must be documented in a Standards Track RFC and extend, rather than replace, the earlier version's XDR. A COMPOUND request carries the minor version the client is requesting.

The RFC also describes an IANA registry for named-attribute definitions. Applications may define named attributes, and registration is encouraged when it can help different implementations interoperate. The document states that the registry has no initial entries and uses the Specification Required policy.
sections.plainLanguage: NFSv4 can gain later minor versions through new Standards Track RFCs that extend the earlier data definitions. Named attributes can also be registered so their meaning is documented for other implementations.
